author_claim: Paul quotes Isaiah 29:14 LXX with customary freedom of citation, substituting ἀθετήσω ('set aside') for κρύψω, possibly influenced by Psalm 33:10 LXX, to apply the prophetic principle regarding the failure of worldly human statesmanship.
short_quote: substituting ἀθετήσω for κρύψω, in accordance with St Paul’s usual freedom of citation.
source_locator: Commentary on 1 Cor 1:19, p. 19 (also Introduction § VI, p. liii)
qualification: Authors note ἀθετήσω possibly comes from Ps 33:10 (LXX 32:10) as a cross-scriptural possibility, rather than a proven direct quotation.
notes: Visibly verified on printed p. 19 (PDF derivative p. 19) and Intro p. liii (PDF derivative p. 11). Self-audit correction incorporated preserving possibility framing.

author_claim: The substituted verb ἀθετήσω is post-classical and frequent in Polybius and the Septuagint, etymologically signifying 'set aside' or 'set at nought' rather than 'destroy.'
short_quote: Its etymological sense is not 'destroy,' but 'set aside' or 'set at nought,'
source_locator: Commentary on 1 Cor 1:19, p. 19 (PDF derivative p. 19)
qualification: Lexical observation on Hellenistic Greek vocabulary in the LXX and Polybius distinguishing ἀθετέω from ἀπόλλυμι.

author_claim: Paul's citation in 1 Corinthians 6:16 is taken directly from the Septuagint of Genesis 2:24, which includes the phrase οἱ δύο ('the two') although it is absent from the original Hebrew Masoretic Text, introduced with φησίν to assert divine authority.
short_quote: The quotation is direct from the LXX, which has οἱ δύο, ... although it is not in the original.
source_locator: Commentary on 1 Cor 6:16, p. 126 (also Introduction § VI, p. liii)
qualification: Authors explain that the subject understood with φησίν depends upon context and may supply either 'God' or ἡ γραφή, asserting divine authority for the quotation.
notes: Visibly verified on printed p. 126 (PDF derivative p. 25) and Intro p. liii (PDF derivative p. 11). Agrees with Matt 19:5, Mark 10:8, Eph 5:31.

author_claim: The verb κολλᾶσθαι with the dative (echoing προσκολλᾶσθαι in Gen 2:24) denotes loyal and permanent adherence resulting in complete spiritual union, set in sharp contrast to temporary physical union with a harlot.
short_quote: to express loyal and permanent adherence, resulting in complete spiritual union. This is placed in marked contrast to the temporary physical union
source_locator: Commentary on 1 Cor 6:16-17, p. 126 (PDF derivative p. 25)
qualification: Notes usage of κολλᾶσθαι in LXX (2 Kings 18:6, Deut 10:20, Sirach 2:3) for adherence to Jehovah.

author_claim: In 1 Corinthians 9:9, the manuscript reading κημώσεις (supported by B* D* G) is original against φιμώσεις, representing a rare verb that scribes readily corrected to match the familiar Septuagint text of Deuteronomy 25:4.
short_quote: How could κημώσεις be so well attested, if it were not original? If it were original it would readily be corrected to the LXX
source_locator: Commentary on 1 Cor 9:9, p. 183 (also Introduction § VII, p. lxii)
qualification: Authors note κημόω is rare in Greek literature (though noun κημός occurs in LXX Ps 31:9, Ezek 19:4, 9), supported by Chrysostom and Theodoret.
notes: Visibly verified on printed p. 183 (PDF derivative p. 33) and Intro p. lxii (PDF derivative p. 18). Text-critical transcriptional probability analysis.

author_claim: Unlike Philo and radical allegorists who rejected the literal sense of Mosaic animal commands, Paul does not reject the literal command of Deuteronomy 25:4 but reasons that it embodies a higher spiritual principle establishing the right of Christian laborers to maintenance.
short_quote: St Paul elsewhere allegorizes the O.T., ... but in neither case does he reject the literal meaning. It is not probable that he does so here
source_locator: Commentary on 1 Cor 9:9-10, p. 184 (PDF derivative p. 34)
qualification: Authors explicitly state that even if πάντως is translated 'altogether,' it need not be pressed to mean that oxen are not cared for at all by God (citing Ps 104:14, 145:9, Matt 6:26).
notes: Visibly verified on printed p. 184. Contrasts Pauline hermeneutics with Philo (De Somniis i. 16, De Sacrificiis 1) and Epistle of Barnabas x. 1-2. Self-audit qualification incorporated.

author_claim: The quotation in 1 Corinthians 10:7 is taken verbatim from the Septuagint of Exodus 32:6, where 'play' (παίζειν) denotes idolatrous choral dances around the golden calf following a sacrificial banquet, serving as a warning against Corinthian participation in pagan temple feasts.
short_quote: The quotation, therefore, indicates an idolatrous banquet followed by idolatrous sport.
source_locator: Commentary on 1 Cor 10:7, pp. 203-204 (PDF derivative pp. 41-42)
qualification: Direct agreement with LXX Exodus 32:6 (Ἐκάθισεν ὁ λαὸς φαγεῖν καὶ πεῖν, καὶ ἀνέστησαν παίζειν). Connects with Calvin's query regarding accessories vs essence of idolatry.

author_claim: In 1 Corinthians 10:6 and 11, the terms τύποι and τυπικῶς do not denote predictive redemptive-historical 'types' (which would imply predestined apostasy for the Corinthians), but historical patterns and warning examples for moral guidance.
short_quote: This confirms the view that τύπος does not mean 'types,' but examples for guidance, 'to the intent that we should not be.'
source_locator: Commentary on 1 Cor 10:6, p. 203 (PDF derivative p. 41)
qualification: Authors argue against rigid typological interpretation, noting that Origen uses τύπος in the sense of example and that the Greek phrase εἰς τὸ μὴ εἶναι expresses moral warning.

author_claim: Robertson and Plummer catalog approximately thirty Old Testament quotations in 1 Corinthians across eleven different biblical books, concluding that about twenty-five are in exact or substantial agreement with the Septuagint.
short_quote: Out of these thirty quotations from the O.T., about twenty-five are in exact or substantial agreement with the LXX
source_locator: Introduction § VI: 'Quotations from the O.T.', p. liii (PDF derivative p. 11)
qualification: Authors note exact figures cannot always be given because some quotations resemble multiple OT passages or conflate two contexts.
notes: Visibly verified on printed p. liii. Identifies 7 exact and 18 substantial LXX agreements.

author_claim: Robertson and Plummer judge that all Old Testament quotations in 1 Corinthians are short and were probably cited from memory, in marked contrast to the long citations in the Epistle to the Hebrews which were in most cases copied from a scroll.
short_quote: All the quotations are short, and it is probable that all of them were made from memory. There are no long citations, such as we have in Hebrews
source_locator: Introduction § VI: 'Quotations from the O.T.', pp. lii-liii (PDF derivative pp. 10-11)
qualification: Authors' compositional hypothesis distinguishing Pauline epistolary citation practice from the literary copying practice in Hebrews.
notes: Visibly verified on printed pp. lii-liii. Directly references Sanday & Headlam's Romans essay (pp. 302-307).`

author_claim: Paul occasionally introduces intentional textual variations into his quotations to produce a wording more suitable for his immediate argument, such as substituting ἀθετήσω for κρύψω in 1 Cor 1:19 (Isa 29:14) and σοφῶν for ἀνθρώπων in 1 Cor 3:20 (Ps 94:11).
short_quote: Sometimes he seems to make changes in order to produce a wording more suitable for his argument
source_locator: Introduction § VI: 'Quotations from the O.T.', p. liii (PDF derivative p. 11)
qualification: Authors attribute these specific variants to conscious argumentative adaptation by the Apostle rather than textual corruption.
notes: Visibly verified on printed p. liii.

author_claim: Where Pauline quotations diverge from the Septuagint, variations sometimes bring the text closer to the Hebrew (e.g. 1 Cor 15:54 / Isa 25:8), or reflect preference for the Hebrew or an unknown Greek translation (1 Cor 1:20, 3:19, 14:25, 15:54), while occasionally diverging from both (1 Cor 2:9, 14:21).
short_quote: Sometimes the variations from the LXX bring the citation closer to the Hebrew, as if the Apostle were consciously or unconsciously guided by the Hebrew
source_locator: Introduction § VI: 'Quotations from the O.T.', pp. liii-liv (PDF derivative pp. 11-12)
qualification: Authors note uncertainty whether guidance by Hebrew text was conscious or unconscious, or mediated via lost Greek versions.
notes: Visibly verified on printed pp. liii-liv.
